cards: The Dutch settle at the Cape of Good Hope, where the Cape San number an estimated 30,000 to 50,000
The Dutch East India Company officially endorses a policy of eradicating the San
Louis Anthing estimates that no more than 500 San are left in all of Bushmanland, facing starvation
The San win a benefit-sharing agreement over their knowledge of the hoodia plant, and their representatives ask to be called by their own nations’ names
Colonel Dent Young finds the first Nok terracotta in a tin mine near the village of Nok
A head used as a scarecrow leads Bernard Fagg to study the culture
Goethe University Frankfurt begins long-term excavations of Nok sites
Ox-mounted ǃUriǁ’aekua defeat and kill Francisco de Almeida at the Battle of Salt River
Georg Schmidt founds Genadendal among the Khoe-speaking peoples, the first mission station in southern Africa
The Kat River Settlement gives Khoekhoe land of their own near the eastern frontier of the Cape Colony
The Cape franchise gives the vote to men meeting a low property test, regardless of colour
Apartheid ends, and with it the racial designation “Coloured” imposed on some Khoekhoe
The Almoravids seize Awdaghast, ending some sixty years of Ghanaian control
Al-Bakri completes his famous description of the gilded royal court
Almoravids sack Koumbi Saleh, reducing Ghana for a time to a tributary
Death of the Almoravid leader Abu Bakr ibn Umar lets the Soninke regain independence
A Tuareg ruling house founds the Sultanate of Agadez in the Aïr Mountains
Tuareg fighters annihilate the French expedition led by Paul Flatters
The French defeat the Kel Ahaggar at the Battle of Tit
After a clash at Tchin-Tabaraden, Tuareg in Mali and Niger rise and claim independence for their homeland
During the Mali War the Azawad Liberation Front captures Kidal and parts of Gao
Umar, son of al-Kanemi, ends the Sayfawa line and founds the dynasty of the shehus
Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr conquers Bornu and destroys Kukawa
French forces kill Rabih at Kousseri; Britain, France and Germany partition the territory
Ibn Battuta visits Mombasa and Kilwa and describes the wealth of the Swahili coast
Letters in Arabic script written at Kilwa, later seized by the Portuguese and kept at Goa, are the oldest known documents in Swahili
The Utendi wa Tambuka, the oldest dated epic poem in Swahili, is composed
A committee of the British East African territories standardises Swahili on the dialect of Zanzibar
Tanzania makes Swahili the language of government and of primary schooling
The first World Kiswahili Language Day is celebrated on 7 July, proclaimed by UNESCO
Isaiah Anozie finds bronzes while digging beside his home
The district officer J. O. Field hands the objects he had bought to the Nigerian Department of Antiquities
Shaw publishes radiocarbon dates placing the sites in the 9th century
New radiocarbon dates from Igbo Isaiah fall between the 10th and 13th centuries
Traditional date for Eri, founder of the Nri line, in Onwuejeogwu’s reconstruction
Ifikuanim, remembered as the first Eze Nri, begins his reign (traditional date)
A British expedition forces the Eze Nri to renounce his ritual powers
Vasco da Gama forces Emir Ibrahim to pay tribute to Portugal
Francisco de Almeida sacks Kilwa and builds Fort Santiago
The Portuguese withdraw their garrison from Kilwa
The ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara become a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Bagauda becomes the first king of Kano, by the Kano Chronicle’s reckoning
Muhammad Rumfa becomes king; he builds the Gidan Rumfa and founds the Kurmi market
Muhammad Alwali II, the last Hausa king of Kano, comes to the throne
The Fulani jihad reaches Kano; Alwali is later driven out and killed at Burum-Burum
Usman dan Fodio’s followers defeat Gobir at Tabkin Kwotto
Alkalawa falls and Sarki Yunfa of Gobir is killed
The Supreme Court of the United States upholds the right of a Santería church in Florida to practise animal sacrifice
UNESCO proclaims Ifa divination a masterpiece of humanity’s oral heritage; the sacred grove of Osogbo becomes a World Heritage Site
The fleet of the Chinese explorer Zheng He visits the town, and Malindi's ruler sends an envoy with a giraffe as a present to China.
Vasco da Gama meets the Malindi authorities, signs a trade agreement, hires a guide for India and erects a padrão; the town has 5,000 to 10,000 people.
King Dom Manuel I of Portugal offers Malindi vassal status; a Portuguese trading post had been set up in 1499 and a factory follows in 1502.
Malindi supports the Portuguese conquest of its rivals Kilwa and Mombasa, and flourishes as merchants, craftsmen and sailors flock to it.
The Portuguese move their main base to Mombasa, surrendered by the Segeju to the Sheikh of Malindi, who moves his court there and rules until 1630.
Ibn Battuta visits and describes Mombasa’s wooden mosques
Mombasa’s rulers try to seize Vasco da Gama’s ships
Francisco de Almeida sacks and burns the town
Nuno da Cunha attacks and burns Mombasa again
The Portuguese capture Mir Ali Bey and the Zimba massacre the inhabitants
The Portuguese begin Fort Jesus and install the ruler of Malindi as sultan
British Punitive Expedition burns Benin City and exiles Oba Ovonramwen
According to local tradition, an Agew family called the Zagwe founds Roha, the later Lalibela
Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi lays waste the district; the Futuh al-Habasha says he burned one of the churches
Haile Selassie makes a pilgrimage to the churches during the Second Italo-Ethiopian War
The churches are first included on the UNESCO World Heritage List
Shelters funded by the EU are put up over five of the churches as a temporary protection
The University of Pretoria begins excavations on Mapungubwe Hill
South Africa institutes the Order of Mapungubwe, its highest honour
The Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape becomes a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Vicente Pegado, captain at Sofala, records the name ‘Symbaoe’ for the stone buildings
Karl Mauch visits the ruins and attributes them to the Queen of Sheba
Gertrude Caton-Thompson’s excavations confirm the site’s African and medieval origin
Independent Zimbabwe takes its name from the ruins
Mali traditionally captures Koumbi Saleh, the former capital of Ghana
Mansa Musa makes his pilgrimage to Mecca, dazzling Cairo with gold
Songhai ruler Sonni Ali captures Timbuktu
Ibn Battuta visits Mogadishu and praises its cloth trade
Yekuno Amlak overthrows the last Zagwe king and founds the Solomonic dynasty
Zara Yaqob defeats the Adal Sultanate at the Battle of Gomit
Ahmad Gran crushes Lebna Dengel at the Battle of Shimbra Kure
Galawdewos, aided by Portuguese musketeers, defeats and kills Ahmad Gran at Wayna Daga
The Zemene Mesafint, the Era of the Princes, begins as regional lords eclipse the emperors
Menelik II routs the Italian army at Adwa, securing Ethiopian independence
Italian forces using aerial bombardment and poison gas capture Addis Ababa
The Derg deposes Haile Selassie; the monarchy is abolished in March 1975
On his way to Mecca he reaches the outskirts of Cairo in July, meets the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and stays three months, giving and spending freely
The kingdom of Mossi invades and conquers Timbuktu; Musa regains the city, builds a rampart and stone fort and stations a standing army there
According to Ibn Khaldun, he sends an envoy to congratulate Abu al-Hasan Ali on the conquest of Tlemcen, which took place in May of that year
Sultan Wali Asma imposes his rule on Hubat, Zeila and the other Muslim states of the region.
Haqq ad-Din I invades Amhara, burns churches, forces conversions and kills the emperor's envoy; Amda Seyon I raids Shewa and Ifat, and Dadader Haqq ad-Din falls at the battle of Marra Biete.
Sabr ad-Din rebels to become 'King of all Ethiopia'; Amda Seyon destroys the capital of Ifat, imprisons him and appoints Jamal ad-Din I in his place.
Haqq ad-Din II, who moved the capital to the Harar plateau and fought over twenty battles with the emperor, dies in battle; his brother Sa'ad ad-Din II succeeds.
Ifat's troops are defeated on the Harar plateau; Sa'ad ad-Din II flees to Zeila and is killed there, by al-Maqrizi's account (another source dates his death to 1410 under Emperor Yeshaq).
Venetian Alvise Cadamosto sees Portuguese traders exchanging horses for slaves on the Senegal coast
Exiled Jolof prince Bemoim is baptised at the court of Joao II in Lisbon
The rump kingdom of Jolof is absorbed into French Senegal
John Hanning Speke reaches the court of Mutesa I
The first Protestant missionaries arrive in Buganda
Christian converts are executed at Namugongo on the orders of Mwanga II
Protestants defeat Catholics at the Battle of Mengo
The Buganda Agreement makes the kingdom a privileged part of the Uganda Protectorate
Troops under Idi Amin storm the kabaka’s palace at Mengo
Uganda’s new constitution abolishes the kingdoms
Oyo begins repeated cavalry invasions of Dahomey
A treaty confirms Dahomey as a tribute-paying vassal of Oyo
New Oyo signs a treaty with the British
Portuguese navigator Diogo Cao reaches the mouth of the Congo
King Nzinga a Nkuwu is baptised as Joao I
Afonso I wins the throne by defeating his half-brother Mpanzu a Kitima
Afonso I writes to Joao III of Portugal protesting the abuses of the slave trade
Jaga invaders drive Alvaro I from his capital until Portuguese troops restore him
Portuguese forces defeat Kongo at Mbwila, killing King Antonio I
Beatriz Kimpa Vita, leader of the Antonian movement, is executed
Pedro IV reoccupies Sao Salvador and nominally reunifies the kingdom
Yendi, the capital since the Gonja wars, is said to be bigger than Kumasi and Salaga.
Dagbon is placed in the neutral Salaga Area, from Yeji to Yendi, agreed between the Germans and the British to forestall conflict.
The Germans defeat the Dagomba at the Battle of Adibo, destroy Yendi and burn the Gbewaa Palace; Eastern Dagbon falls to German Togoland.
Yaa Naa Andani II dies in August; the British and Germans split Dagbon between German Togoland and the Gold Coast.
On 7 April Friedrich Rigler's German expedition attacks the Dagomba who had fled to Sang in British territory, kills at least 83, among them Andani's son Idi, and installs Alasan as Yaa Naa.
Sultan Badlay is defeated and killed by Zara Yaqob at the Battle of Gomit
Sultan Abu Bakr moves the capital from Dakkar to Harar
Imam Ahmad routs Lebna Dengel's larger Ethiopian army at Shimbra Kure
Imam Ahmad is killed at Wayna Daga and his coalition collapses
Nur ibn Mujahid kills Emperor Gelawdewos at the Battle of Fatagar
Sarsa Dengel defeats Sultan Muhammad ibn Nasir at the Webi River
The dynasty withdraws to the oasis of Aussa
Jesuit Gonçalo da Silveira converts the Mwene Mutapa and is then killed at court
Gatsi Rusere cedes mining rights to the Portuguese in return for military help
The Portuguese depose Kapararidze and install Mavura as a vassal ruler
The Portuguese suppress the last reduced Mutapa kingdom in the Zambezi valley
Sunni Ali begins his reign and launches campaigns of conquest
Sunni Ali takes Timbuktu from the Tuareg
Muhammad Ture defeats Sunni Baru and takes the title Askia
Askia Muhammad sets out on his pilgrimage to Mecca
Askia Muhammad is deposed by his son Askia Musa
Civil war divides the Songhai Empire
Judar Pasha's Moroccan army routs Askia Ishaq II at the Battle of Tondibi
Ntare V dies; Kahaya II is installed with Nuwa Mbaguta's support
The Ankole Agreement enlarges the kingdom within the Uganda Protectorate
Charles Gasyonga II succeeds Kahaya II
Uganda's new constitution abolishes the kingdom
Kabalega wins the throne and builds the standing abarusura army
Kabalega forces Samuel Baker to retreat after fighting at Masindi
British and Ganda forces invade Bunyoro
Kabalega is captured in Lango and exiled to the Seychelles
A referendum returns two 'lost counties' from Buganda to Bunyoro
The monarchy is abolished; it is restored as a cultural institution in 1993
The ngola sends envoys to Portugal asking for missionaries
A Portuguese embassy under Paulo Dias de Novais arrives in Ndongo
Ngola Kilombo kia Kasenda has the Portuguese at Kabasa killed, starting a long war
Ndongo and Matamba rout a Portuguese army at the Battle of Lukala
Njinga Mbande negotiates peace in Luanda and is baptised as Ana de Sousa
Portugal makes war on Njinga and sets up rival kings at Pungo Andongo
Njinga and her Dutch allies defeat the Portuguese at the Battle of Kombi
The Portuguese take Pungo Andongo, ending the Kingdom of Ndongo
Kigeli IV Rwabugiri dies on campaign after decades of expansion
The Coup of Rucunshu brings Yuhi V Musinga to the throne
Rwanda accepts German protection and joins German East Africa
Belgium deposes Musinga and installs Mutara III Rudahigwa
Mutara III dies and the Hutu revolution begins
A UN-supervised referendum confirms the abolition of the monarchy
Kasongo Nyembo is captured after years of resisting Free State and Belgian rule
The Portuguese found Cacheu, a key coastal port for Kaabu's slave trade
Futa Jallon forces besiege and destroy Kansala, ending the empire
Radama I's treaty with Britain ends slave exports and brings arms and training
Ranavalona I bans Christianity; the Malagasy Bible is published
Ranavalona II and Rainilaiarivony are baptised; the royal talismans are burned
The Code of 305 Articles is promulgated
French troops under General Duchesne take Antananarivo
France abolishes the monarchy and exiles Ranavalona III
The Capuchin Bernardo Ungaro baptises the king as Afonso, and 6,000 of his subjects with him; a civil war between Christian and non-Christian parties follows his death.
Queen Verónica I of Ndongo-Matamba promises by treaty to stop trading with the Vili merchants operating in the Mbundu-speaking regions of eastern Angola.
French missionaries under Abbé Liévin-Bonaventure Proyart find a king who came to power only after a seven-year interregnum managed by a regent, the Mani Boman.
King Buatu dies and no successor is elected for over a hundred years; the Nganga Mvumbi holds residual royal authority.
Sipopa leads a Lozi rising that ends Kololo rule
Lubosi, later called Lewanika, becomes Litunga
Lewanika signs the Lochner Concession with the British South Africa Company
Italian arbitration fixes the border with Angola, cutting off western lands
The Barotseland Agreement brings the kingdom into independent Zambia
Zambia abrogates the agreement and renames the area Western Province
Egypt conquers Kordofan, cutting Darfur's eastern trade
Al-Zubayr defeats Sultan Ibrahim at Manawashi and Darfur is annexed by Egypt
Ali Dinar returns to El Fasher and restores the sultanate
Anglo-Egyptian force wins at Birinjiya; Ali Dinar is killed in November
Agaja conquers the Kingdom of Allada
Dahomey conquers Whydah, the leading slave-trading port of the coast
Ghezo overthrows Adandozan and revives royal power
A Dahomean assault on Abeokuta is repulsed with heavy losses
French troops under Colonel Dodds take Abomey
Behanzin surrenders and is exiled to Martinique
Sultan Ali's armies sack Massenya, capital of the rival sultanate of Bagirmi
An Anglo-French convention places Wadai in the French sphere
A French column captures Abéché and installs Adam Asil as a client sultan
Sultan Dud Murra surrenders after years of resistance from the countryside
Asante coalition defeats Denkyira at Feyiase, gaining access to coastal trade
Asante army annihilates a British-led force at Nsamankow, killing Governor MacCarthy
A British-led coalition aided by Congreve rockets defeats Asante at Katamansu
Treaty of Peace fixes the River Pra as the southern limit of Asante influence
Sir Garnet Wolseley's expedition enters Kumasi and burns the capital
British occupy Kumasi without a fight and depose Asantehene Prempeh I
Yaa Asantewaa leads the War of the Golden Stool against British rule
Asante is formally annexed as a British crown colony
Mwezi IV submits to German rule in the Treaty of Kiganda
Belgian troops occupy Burundi during the First World War
UPRONA wins the elections; its leader, Prince Louis Rwagasore, is assassinated
Burundi becomes independent as a constitutional monarchy under Mwambutsa IV
Michel Micombero deposes Ntare V and proclaims a republic
Dombo defeats Mutapa and Portuguese forces at the Battle of Maungwe
Rozvi forces destroy the Portuguese settlement at Dambarare and sweep away the interior fairs
The Portuguese fair at Masekesa in Manica falls, shortly before Dombo's death
Ngolo Diarra, a former tonjon, seizes power and founds the Diarra dynasty
Mungo Park reaches the Niger at Ségou during the reign of Monzon Diarra
Seku Amadu’s victory at Noukouma begins the Massina jihad that takes Djenné
Umar Tall’s army defeats the Bamana at Woïtala
Umar Tall takes Ségou and makes it the capital of the Toucouleur Empire
Swaziland becomes a protectorate of the South African Republic
The Partition Proclamation leaves the Swazi only about a third of their land
Swaziland becomes independent under Sobhuza II
Sobhuza II repeals the constitution and bans political parties
Mswati III renames the country the Kingdom of Eswatini
British forces take the Cape after the Battle of Muizenberg
Britain reoccupies the colony after the Battle of Blaauwberg
About 4,000 British settlers arrive in the Eastern Cape
Slavery is abolished across the colony
A parliament is elected on a non-racial property franchise
The Cape receives responsible government under John Molteno
Cecil Rhodes becomes prime minister of the Cape
The colony becomes the Cape Province of the Union of South Africa
Usman dan Fodio makes his hijra to Gudu and declares jihad against the Hausa kings
Jihad forces storm Alkalawa, the Gobir capital, killing Sultan Yunfa
Dan Fodio dies; his son Muhammad Bello becomes Sultan of Sokoto
Britain charters the Royal Niger Company
Frederick Lugard proclaims the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria
British forces take Kano in February and occupy Sokoto in March
Sultan Attahiru I is killed fighting the British at Burmi in July
Shaka seizes leadership of the Zulu chiefdom with Mthethwa support
Shaka is assassinated at Dukuza by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana
Boer forces defeat Dingane’s army at the Battle of Blood River
Cetshwayo defeats his brother Mbuyazi at the Battle of Ndondakusuka
The Zulu win at Isandlwana but are defeated at Ulundi
Cetshwayo is restored to part of Zululand; civil war follows
Britain annexes Zululand as a British colony
The British Crown dissolves the African Company of Merchants and places its Gold Coast forts under Charles MacCarthy, governor of Sierra Leone.
MacCarthy is killed and most of his force wiped out in a battle with Asante forces; a British, Fante and Accra force defeats an Asante invasion of the coast in 1826.
Commander Henry Worsley Hill negotiates the Bond of 1844 with Fante and other chiefs, who submit murder and robbery to British jurisdiction.
Sir Garnet Wolseley's force occupies and burns Kumasi in January; the coastal protectorate is proclaimed the Gold Coast Colony on 24 July.
A second British expedition occupies Kumasi, makes Asante a protectorate and exiles the asantehene.
After the War of the Golden Stool of 1900 Asante is proclaimed a colony and the Northern Territories a protectorate under the governor of the Gold Coast.
Rioting in Accra and other towns over ex-servicemen's pensions, housing and the foreign hold on the economy; Nkrumah and the UGCC's 'Big Six' are detained.
On 6 March the Colony of the Gold Coast becomes independent as Ghana.
Ibadan comes into existence as a war camp for warriors from Oyo, Ifẹ and Ijebu, amid the turmoil in which Old Oyo, Ijaye and Owu disappear; by the end of the year it dominates the Yoruba region.
The armies of Ibadan decisively defeat the Sokoto Caliphate's attempt to expand into the south, halting its progress.
The Church Missionary Society sends David and Anna Hinderer, who found a mission and church in the city in 1853 and open its first Western school.
On 15 August Fijabi, the Baale of Ibadan, signs a treaty with George C. Denton, acting Governor of Lagos Colony, and the Ibadan area becomes a British protectorate.
American Colonization Society settlers land at Cape Mesurado, later Monrovia
Liberia declares independence under President Joseph Jenkins Roberts
Firestone receives a vast rubber concession
A forced labour scandal forces President Charles King to resign
William Tubman begins a presidency lasting until 1971
Samuel Doe’s coup ends True Whig Party rule
Charles Taylor’s invasion starts the first Liberian civil war
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf becomes Africa’s first elected female head of state
The Sand River Convention recognises Boer independence north of the Vaal
Pretoria becomes the seat of government
The Boers defeat a British force at Majuba Hill and regain self-government
Gold is discovered on the Witwatersrand and Johannesburg is founded
The Jameson Raid ends in surrender at Doornkop
The Second Boer War begins after a Transvaal ultimatum expires
The Treaty of Vereeniging makes the republic the Transvaal Colony
Britain defeats Boers under Andries Pretorius at Boomplaats and rules the Orange River Sovereignty
The Bloemfontein Convention recognises the independence of the Orange Free State
Moshoeshoe cedes land west of the Caledon River in the Treaty of Thaba Bosiu
Britain annexes the diamond fields of Griqualand West
Defensive alliance with the South African Republic
Bloemfontein falls to Lord Roberts and Britain annexes the state as the Orange River Colony
The Treaty of Vereeniging ends the Second Boer War and the republic
Majid bin Said becomes sultan of Zanzibar on the division of Sayyid Said’s realm
The Canning Award confirms Zanzibar’s separation from Oman
Barghash closes the Zanzibar slave market under British pressure
A German squadron forces Barghash to recognise German claims on the mainland
Zanzibar and Pemba become a British protectorate
The Anglo-Zanzibar War ends in under an hour
Zanzibar becomes independent under Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah
The Zanzibar Revolution overthrows the sultan; union with Tanganyika follows
Henry Morton Stanley begins building stations on the Congo River for Leopold
Leopold proclaims the Congo Free State after the Berlin Conference
The Yeke king Msiri is killed and Katanga is secured for the state
The Force Publique defeats the Swahili-Arab traders of the eastern Congo
Roger Casement’s report is published and the Congo Reform Association is founded
Belgium annexes the territory as the Belgian Congo
Tafari Makonnen is born on 23 July in the village of Ejersa Goro, in the Hararghe province of Ethiopia
After Lij Iyasu is deposed on 27 September, Tafari is proclaimed Crown Prince and Regent Plenipotentiary under Empress Zewditu
Following the death of Empress Zewditu he is crowned emperor on 2 November at the Cathedral of St. George in Addis Ababa, taking the regnal name Haile Selassie I
He introduces Ethiopia's first written constitution on 16 July, providing for a bicameral legislature
Defeated at the Battle of Maychew, he leaves Ethiopia on 2 May and addresses the League of Nations on the Italian invasion
He enters Addis Ababa on 5 May, exactly five years after the Italian forces had entered the city
He presides over the formation of the Organisation of African Unity and is elected its first chairperson
The Derg, a committee of junior officers and enlisted men, deposes the 82-year-old emperor on 12 September
A governor-general is created for France’s West African colonies at Saint-Louis
Ernest Roume’s decree gives the federation its own administration and budget in Dakar
Blaise Diagne leads a recruitment drive for the First World War
Vichy forces repel a British and Free French attack on Dakar
French troops fire on tirailleurs at the Thiaroye camp near Dakar
The indigénat and forced labour are abolished and Africans become citizens
The loi-cadre Defferre gives power to elected territorial assemblies
Guinea votes for independence; the federation is wound up
Henry Sylvester Williams’s Pan-African Conference meets in London; W. E. B. Du Bois drafts its address
Marcus Garvey founds the Universal Negro Improvement Association in Jamaica
Du Bois’s first Pan-African Congress meets in Paris during the peace conference
Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia unites Africans and the diaspora in protest
The Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester demands independence for Africa
Thirty-two independent states found the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa
The African Union replaces the Organisation of African Unity
The Union of South Africa is proclaimed, with Louis Botha as prime minister
The South African Native National Congress, later the ANC, is founded at Bloemfontein
The Natives Land Act restricts African land ownership to reserves
South African forces conquer German South West Africa
The Statute of Westminster confirms the Union’s legislative independence
D. F. Malan’s National Party wins power and begins apartheid
Police kill 69 protesters at Sharpeville; white voters approve a republic
The Union becomes the Republic of South Africa on 31 May
Mandela helps to found the African National Congress Youth League and sits on its executive committee
He opens the Defiance Campaign at a Durban rally, is arrested, and is elected president of the ANC's Transvaal branch
Acquitted in the Treason Trial, he co-founds Umkhonto we Sizwe, which announces itself with 57 bombings in December
At the Rivonia Trial he is found guilty of sabotage and conspiracy and sentenced to life imprisonment
President F. W. de Klerk announces his unconditional release, and he leaves Victor Verster Prison on 11 February
The ANC wins 63% of the vote in the first multiracial general election, and he is inaugurated as President of South Africa
He retires after one term and is succeeded by his deputy, Thabo Mbeki
Mandela dies at his home in Houghton at the age of 95
Anténor Firmin publishes On the Equality of Human Races, a rebuttal of Arthur de Gobineau
Jane Nardal’s article “Internationalisme noir”, on race consciousness in the African diaspora, lays a philosophical foundation
Paulette Nardal and Leo Sajou start La Revue du Monde Noir, a journal in English and French
Aimé Césaire first uses the word négritude in its present sense, in the third issue of L’Étudiant noir
Léon Damas publishes the anthology Poètes d’expression française 1900–1945
Senghor’s Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache appears with Jean-Paul Sartre’s preface “Black Orpheus”
Wole Soyinka mocks Négritude’s “duikeritude”, and Paulette Nardal complains of the neglect of her and her sister’s part
The National Party wins power and begins to build apartheid into law
The ANC and the South African Indian Congress launch the Defiance Campaign against Unjust Laws
The Congress of the People adopts the Freedom Charter at Kliptown
Police kill 69 protesters at Sharpeville, and the ANC and the PAC are banned
Nelson Mandela and seven others are sentenced to life imprisonment in the Rivonia Trial
The Soweto uprising begins with a schoolchildren’s march against teaching in Afrikaans
F. W. de Klerk unbans the liberation movements, and Mandela is freed after 27 years
South Africa holds its first election open to all, and Mandela becomes president
The Union becomes the Republic of South Africa and leaves the Commonwealth
Nelson Mandela is sentenced to life imprisonment at the end of the Rivonia Trial
Police fire on protesting students in Soweto, setting off a national uprising
F. W. de Klerk unbans the ANC; Mandela is released after 27 years in prison
The first democratic elections make Nelson Mandela president
A new constitution with a Bill of Rights is adopted
Police kill 34 striking miners at Marikana
The ANC loses its majority and forms a Government of National Unity
The Rwandan Revolution: Hutu activists kill Tutsi and burn their houses, driving more than 100,000 people into neighbouring countries.
On 1 July Rwanda, separated from Burundi after a 1961 referendum abolished the monarchy, becomes independent under President Grégoire Kayibanda.
Juvénal Habyarimana takes power in a military coup; pro-Hutu discrimination continues with less violence and more prosperity.
The Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed of Tutsi refugees, invades northern Rwanda from Uganda, beginning the Rwandan Civil War.
On 6 April Habyarimana's plane is shot down near Kigali; within hours the genocide begins, killing 500,000 to 1,000,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about 100 days.
The RPF takes control of the whole country, ending the genocide; some two million Hutu flee to Zaïre and other neighbours.
Paul Kagame, the RPF's former commander, becomes president; a constitution follows in 2003 after a national referendum.
On 25 January the Democratic Republic of the Congo severs diplomatic relations over Rwanda's support for the M23 rebellion after the Goma offensive.
Uganda becomes independent on 9 October under Prime Minister Milton Obote
Troops under Idi Amin storm the Kabaka’s palace at Mengo
A republican constitution abolishes the kingdoms
Idi Amin seizes power in a military coup
Amin expels the country’s Asian community
Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles take Kampala and overthrow Amin
The National Resistance Army takes Kampala and Museveni becomes president
The kingdoms are restored as cultural institutions
Tanganyika and Zanzibar unite on 26 April; the name Tanzania is adopted in October
The Arusha Declaration launches ujamaa socialism
Dodoma is designated the future capital
TANU and the Afro-Shirazi Party merge as Chama Cha Mapinduzi
Tanzanian forces capture Kampala and overthrow Idi Amin
Samia Suluhu Hassan becomes the first woman president
On 11 November the Cabinet of Rhodesia issues a unilateral declaration of independence from the United Kingdom; Governor Sir Humphrey Gibbs dismisses Ian Smith and his ministers, who ignore him.
On 12 November United Nations Security Council Resolution 216 calls on all states not to recognise 'this illegal racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia'.
On 28 April seven ZANLA insurgents are cornered and killed near Sinoia, the first engagement of the Rhodesian Bush War, kept by ZANU as Chimurenga Day.
On 2 March Rhodesia declares itself a republic after a referendum of 1969 severed the last ties with the Crown by 61,130 votes to 14,327.
On 21 December ZANLA insurgents under Rex Nhongo cross from Mozambique and raid a commercial farm, opening the raids on white farmers across the north-east.
The end of Portuguese rule in Mozambique after the Carnation Revolution leaves Rhodesia almost surrounded by hostile states.
On 3 September ZIPRA fighters shoot down the Air Rhodesia Viscount Hunyani near Kariba with a surface-to-air missile and kill 10 of its 18 survivors.
On 1 June under the Internal Settlement Abel Muzorewa becomes the first black prime minister of the renamed Zimbabwe Rhodesia; the Lancaster House Agreement ends UDI in December.

The Derg is established as the Coordinating Committee of the Armed Forces, Police and Territorial Army by junior and mid-level officers; announced on 28 June, it elects Major Mengistu Haile Mariam chairman.
On 12 September the Derg deposes and imprisons Emperor Haile Selassie during nationwide protests; three days later it renames itself the Provisional Military Administrative Council.
On 23 November the Derg removes and kills its chairman, Lieutenant General Aman Andom, with some of his supporters and 60 officials of the imperial government, the Massacre of the Sixty.
On 4 March the land reform 'Land to the Tiller' nationalises all rural land and abolishes tenancy; the monarchy is formally abolished the same month, and Haile Selassie dies on 27 August.
On 23 September the Red Terror begins after a failed attempt on Mengistu's life attributed to the EPRP; in less than two years up to 980,000 people are killed by the highest estimates.
On 3 February Chairman Tafari Benti is killed in a shootout and Mengistu takes power; Vice-Chairman Atnafu Abate is executed with 40 officers on 13 November; Somalia invades the Ogaden.

On 22 February the Derg government ends after a referendum approves the constitution of the People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia; the Derg is formally abolished in September, its members keeping power.
British Somaliland is independent for five days, then unites with Somalia
Government forces bombard Hargeisa and Burao in the war with the SNM
Independence is declared at Burao on 18 May
The Borama conference chooses Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal as president
A referendum approves the constitution and independence
Silanyo defeats the incumbent president and power passes peacefully
Somaliland forces are driven from positions around Las Anod
Israel becomes the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland
